question: Immersion syndrome occurs due to ?
explanation:
Vagal inhibition
Types of drowning
Drowning is classified as (1) typical and (2) atypical.
1. Typical drowning (wet drowning)
 Typical drowning refers to obstruction of air passages and lungs by
inhalation of water or other fluid. Therefore it is also called wet
drowning and findings offluid and froth are present in PM
examination. Typical drowning may be :-
i. Fresh water drowning : In fresh water drowning large quantities of
water cross the alveolar membrane into circulation causing
hypervolaemia and hemodilution. RBCs imbibe water and burst
(hemolysis) with liberation of potossium. Therefore, heart is exposed
to volume overload, potassium excess, sodium deficit
(hyponatremia), and anoxia. Anoxia and hyperkalemia cause
ventricular fibrillation and death in 4-5 minutes.
ii. Salt water drowning : Hypertonicity of inhaled water causes loss of
fluid from circulation into the lungs giving rise fulminating pulmonary
edema with progressive hypovolaemia, circulatary shock, and
eventually cardiac standstill (asystole) with death in 8-12 minutes.
2. Atypical drowning
It refers to drowning in which even after submersion of body in
water, little or no water anters respiratory passages and lungs.
Hence typical findings of wet drowning in the form of froth and
oedema aquosum of lungs are not found. Atypical drowning may be
:-
i. Dry drowning : On contact with water, especially cold water, there
results intense laryngospasm, so that water does not enter the
lungs. Death is due to asphyxia because of laryngospasm.
ii. Immersion syndrome (hydrocution/submersion inhibition/vagal
inhibition) : Sudden death occurs due to vagal inhibition as a result
of (a) sudden impact with cold water, (b) duck diving (falling in water
with feet first), and (c) horizontal entry in water with impact on
epigastrium.
iii. Submersion of unconscious : If person is unconscious since before
submersion in water, little or no water enters respiratory passages. It
may occur in MI, cerebrovascular accident, hypertension, epilepsy,
cerebral aneurysm and in drunk state.
iv. Near drowning (secondary drowning syndrome/post immersion
syndrome) : In this drowning is survived and death occurs at a later
stage after removal from water. Either the person himself comes out
of water or he is recovered alive, but due to complications of
submersion, he dies at a later stage. It is due to hypoxic
encephalopathy and fibrosing alveolitis. The death occurs due to
combined effect of cerebral hypoxia, pulmonary edema, aspiration
pneumonitis, electrolyte disturbances and metabolic acidosis.

at birth.
2) Maceration : Maceration is a process of aseptic autolysis. It
occurs when a dead fetus remains in the uterus for 3-4 days
surrounded by liquor amnii but with exclusion of air. Skin slippage is
the earliest sign (occurs within 12 hours). There is gas in the great
vessels and chambers of heart (Robert's sign). Except for lung and
uterus, which remain unchanged for a long time, all other organs
become soft, oedematous and loose there morphology. The one
important radiological sign suggestive of maceration is 'Spaulding's
sign' i.e. skull bones override each other. The smell is somewhat
rancid.
3) Putrefaction (decomposition) : If the membranes are ruptured
after death of fetus and air gains entry into liquor amnii, fetus
undergoes putrefaction instead of maceration. Body is greenish, foul
smelling and bloated.
4) Mummification : It results when there is deficient blood supply,
scanty liquor and no air enters uterus. Body is thin, shrivelled dark
brown and emitting smell like rotten cheese.

question: Following is not true about adipocere formation ?

options.A: It is a modification of putrefaction
options.B: It is developed in presence of air
options.C: It occurs in dead bodies lying in water
options.D: Body has an offensive sweet smell

explanation:
It is developed in presence of air
Adipocere formation (saponification).
Adipocere is a modification of putrefaction, which occurs in the
absence of air. That is when there is excessive moisture (humidity)
and warnth (warm temperature), but absence of air i.e. warm humid
climate, normal putrefaction does not occur, rather saponification
occurs.
Thus adipocese formation occurs in dead bodies which are lying in
water (immered in water) or burned in damp lay soil.
Saponification (adipocer formation) is the conversion of dead body
into soft, fatty waxy substance due to conversion of unsaturated
liquid fats to saturated solid fats under the influence of intrinsic
lipase and lecithinase produced by Cl. perfringens. The process
involves gradual hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fats into
higher fatty acids which combine with calcium and ammonium ions
to form insoluble soaps. Ultimately, palmitic, oleic, stearic and
hydroxystearic acids are formed, mixture of these is known as
adipocere.
Adipocere formation starts in subcutaneous fat and is marked in
areas having excessive fat, eg. cheeks, female breast, buttocks and
abdomen. Slowly the whole body including muscles and internal
viscera change into adipocere. Adipocere has offensive or sweetish
smell, however in early stages, smell is ammonical.
Body is converted into soft, waxy and brittle substance, it floats on
water, it can be cut easily, it dissolves in alcohol and ethers, and it
melts on heating. Facial features and injuries on body are well
preserved, thus identfication of body and determination cause of
death (in case of injury) are possible.
Normally adipocere formation requires 3 weeks to upto 3 to 6
months. However shortest recorded period in india is 3 days 22
hours. In india, it has been observed to begin within 4-5 days.
Adipocere may persist for years or decades. Adipocere does not
occur in foetus less than 7 month's.
Medicolegal importance : (i) Identification of body (facial features are
preserved), (ii) cause of death (injury marks are preserved), (iii) time
since death can be estimated.

question: Mummification is enhanced by ?
explanation:
Dry and hot air
Mummification
It is a modification of putrefaction, which occurs in the absence of
moisture. That is when there is excess air and warmth but no
moisture (humidity), i.e. hot dry and windy climate, mummification
takes place in place of normal putrefaction. Thus mummification
occurs in deserts, especially in summer and also in bodies buried in
shallow grave in sandy soil.
Mummification is characterized by dessication or drying of the dead
body. There is drying, dehydration and shriveling of dead body. It
proceeds from exterior to interior. Therefore first to be involved is
skin, especially of exposed body parts like lips, nose tip, hands
(fingers) and feet (toes). The skin is shrunken, contracted, dry,
brittle, leathery, streched across bony prominences and rusty brown
to black in color. Internal viscera also dry up, darken in color and
blend with each other to form a single mass. Body emits smell like
rotten cheese. Facial features and injuries are well preserved, thus
identification of body and cause of death can be determined (like
adipocere formation).
Time required for mummification varies between 3 months - 2 years.
If properly preserved, a mummified body can remain for years.
Chronic arsenic or antimony poisoning favor mummification.
Medicolegal importance : (i) Identification of body (facial features are
preserved), (ii) cause of death (injury marks are preserved), (iii) time
since death can be estimated.

question: When group of muscles of dead body were in state of strong contration immediately prior to death and remain so even after death, this is termed as ?

Cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor) is defined as the condition
wherein a group of muscles, which were in contraction or spasm at
the time of death, continue to be in spasm even after death, without
the stage of primary relaxation.
It is a condition in which the muscles of the body which were in a
state of contraction immediately before death, continue to be so after
death without passing through the stage of primary relaxation. 
Cadaveric spasm, being an antemortem phenomenon, reflects the
last act of the subject performed before and at the time of his death.
The cause and manner of death may be judged. 
It may be due to exhausted ATP in the affected muscles with the
persistence of contraction even after death and the resulting failure
of the chemical processes required for active muscular relaxation to
occur during molecular death. Adrenocortical exhaustion, which
impairs resynthesis of ATP may be the possible cause

question: Which of following tests in used to detect semen?
explanation:
**Barberio's test** is a confirmatory chemical test used to detect the presence of semen in forensic examination. It works by detecting **spermine**, a polyamine present in high concentration in seminal fluid. When a saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of **picric acid** is added to a semen sample, it reacts with spermine to form **yellow, needle-shaped crystals of spermine picrate**, which are observed microscopically. This makes it a valuable test in cases of suspected sexual assault and other medicolegal investigations, often used alongside the **Florence test** (which detects choline using potassium iodide solution).

The other options are incorrect because they detect different substances:
- **Phenolphthalein test (Kastle-Meyer test)** is a presumptive test for **blood**, detecting the peroxidase activity of hemoglobin (turns pink).
- **Reine's test** is not a recognized standard test for semen detection (a distractor).
- **Paraffin test (Dermal nitrate test)** is used to detect **gunshot residue** (nitrites/nitrates) on the hands of a suspected shooter, not semen.

question: Amyl Nitrate is used as an antidote in...poisoning :
explanation:
Amyl nitrite is a key component of the cyanide antidote kit, where it acts by inducing methemoglobinemia. Cyanide is lethal because it binds to the ferric iron (Fe³⁺) of cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, halting cellular respiration and causing histotoxic hypoxia. Amyl nitrite oxidizes hemoglobin's ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) to ferric iron, forming methemoglobin, which has a high affinity for cyanide and draws it away from cytochrome oxidase to form cyanmethemoglobin, restoring cellular oxygen utilization. This is typically followed by sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate, the latter converting cyanide to nontoxic thiocyanate for renal excretion.

The other options are incorrect: CO₂ poisoning (A) causes asphyxiation by displacing oxygen and is managed simply with fresh air and ventilation. Carbon monoxide poisoning (B) is treated with 100% oxygen or hyperbaric oxygen, not amyl nitrite—in fact, inducing methemoglobinemia in CO poisoning would be harmful as it further reduces oxygen-carrying capacity. Nitric acid (D) is a corrosive agent requiring decontamination and supportive care, not an antidote like amyl nitrite.

question: Nysten's rule pertains to ?
explanation:

Rigor mortis
It is defined as contraction, stiffening, shortenig and opacity of
muscles after death.
It occurs after molecular (cellular) death. In tropical countries (e.g.
india), it begins 1-2 hours after death, takes further 2 hours to
develop, and lasts for 18-36 hours in summer and 24-48 hours in
winter.
In temperate countries, it begins in 3-6 hours, takes further 2-3 hours
to develop and lasts for 2-3 days.
All muscles of body are involved, i.e. voluntary or involuntary.
However, it does not start in all muscles simultaneously (nysten's
rule).
Involuntary muscles (heart) are involved first than voluntary muscles.
Sequence of muscles involvement is as follows : Heart > upper
eyelid > neck > jaw > face > chest > upper limb > abdomen > lower
limb > finger and toes.
It passes off in the same order in which it has appeared.

question: For phage typing, how many phages of staphylococcus aureus are used ?
explanation:
Phage typing of *Staphylococcus aureus* is an epidemiological tool that uses a standardized **international set of 23 bacteriophages** to subtype strains based on their susceptibility to lysis by specific phages. Each phage recognizes particular surface receptors on the bacterial cell wall, and the unique pattern of lysis (phage type) helps trace the source and spread of infection during outbreaks, such as in hospital settings or food poisoning incidents. The 23 phages are grouped into four major lytic groups (Group I, II, III, and a miscellaneous group), allowing strains to be characterized by their reaction profile.

This makes option **D (23)** correct, reflecting the basic phage set adopted by the International Subcommittee on Phage Typing of Staphylococci.

The other options are incorrect because they do not correspond to the standardized international set: options A (12), B (15), and C (20) are arbitrary numbers and do not match the established panel. While phage typing has largely been supplanted by molecular methods like PFGE and MLST, the classic figure of 23 remains the examiner-favored fact for *S. aureus* phage typing.

question: Enteric fever is caused by: September 2005
explanation:
Enteric fever is a systemic febrile illness caused by **Salmonella enterica** serotypes that are adapted to humans, and it encompasses both typhoid and paratyphoid fever. Specifically, it is caused by *Salmonella* Typhi (typhoid fever) as well as *Salmonella* Paratyphi A, B, and C (paratyphoid fever), making option D the most complete and correct answer.

The mechanism involves ingestion of the organism via contaminated food or water, after which the bacteria invade the intestinal mucosa, are taken up by macrophages, and disseminate via the lymphatics and bloodstream (bacteremia). This systemic spread accounts for the characteristic features of stepladder fever, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots, and potential complications like intestinal perforation. Paratyphoid fever (caused by *S.* Paratyphi A and B) is generally clinically milder than typhoid but produces a similar overall syndrome.

Options A, B, and C are each individually correct but incomplete, as enteric fever is not caused by any single one of these organisms alone. Since all three (and S. Paratyphi C) can produce the enteric fever syndrome, choosing only one would exclude the others, so **"All of the above" (D)** is the precise answer.

question: Transmission of cholera is through ?

options.C: Contaminated food by vomits of case

explanation:
Cholera, caused by *Vibrio cholerae* (chiefly serogroups O1 and O139), is transmitted primarily through the **fecal-oral route**, meaning all the listed modes contribute to its spread. The organism is shed in massive numbers in the watery "rice-water" stools of cases and carriers, and also in vomitus, allowing it to contaminate water sources, food, and surfaces. **Fecally contaminated water** is the most important vehicle, especially in epidemics where sewage mixes with drinking water; **fecally contaminated food** (seafood, vegetables washed in contaminated water) spreads it as well; and **food contaminated by vomits** of a patient can also transmit the bacterium.

Once ingested in a sufficient infective dose, the bacteria colonize the small intestine and produce cholera toxin, which activates adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP and causing massive secretory diarrhea and dehydration. Options A, B, and C are each individually correct but incomplete, since none alone captures the full range of transmission routes. Therefore, **D (All of the above)** is the most accurate answer, reflecting that cholera spreads through multiple fecal-oral pathways involving both water and food.

question: Safety pin appearance is seen in ?
explanation:
**Vibrio parahaemolyticus** demonstrates the characteristic "safety pin" appearance due to **bipolar staining**, where the organism stains more intensely at its two poles than in the center, resembling a closed safety pin. This is a feature shared by several *Vibrio* species, which are curved, comma-shaped Gram-negative rods that exhibit darting motility via a single polar flagellum.

The bipolar staining results from the uneven distribution of cytoplasmic contents and the way the dye concentrates at the ends of the bacterial cell, giving the central portion a clearer, vacuolated look. Clinically, *V. parahaemolyticus* is a halophilic (salt-loving) organism associated with **seafood-related gastroenteritis**, and its pathogenicity is linked to the Kanagawa phenomenon (beta-hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar due to thermostable direct hemolysin).

Among the other options: **Vibrio vulnificus** (A), though also a *Vibrio*, is classically associated with wound infections and septicemia in patients with liver disease rather than being the textbook answer for safety pin appearance. **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** (C) is a Gram-negative rod known for pigment production (pyocyanin), fruity odor, and biofilm formation, not bipolar staining. **H. influenzae** (D) is a small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacillus requiring factors X and V for growth, with no safety pin morphology. *(Note: Yersinia pestis is the most classic "safety pin"/bipolar staining organism overall, but among the given choices, Vibrio parahaemolyticus is correct.)*

question: Milk ring test is done to detect which organism present in milk?
explanation:
The **Milk Ring Test (MRT)** is a screening test used to detect *Brucella* antibodies in milk, primarily for surveillance of **bovine brucellosis** (caused by *Brucella abortus*) in dairy herds. The test works on the principle of agglutination: a stained *Brucella* antigen (hematoxylin or tetrazolium-stained) is added to a milk sample, and if anti-*Brucella* antibodies are present, they bind the antigen and become trapped in the fat globules. As the cream rises, it carries the agglutinated antigen-antibody complexes upward, forming a colored **ring at the top (cream layer)**, indicating a positive result. This makes MRT a valuable, inexpensive tool for monitoring brucellosis at the herd level rather than testing individual animals.

The other options are incorrect because they are detected by different methods: **Bordetella** (whooping cough) is diagnosed via nasopharyngeal culture/PCR; **Bartonella** is identified by serology, culture, or PCR (associated with cat-scratch disease); and **Salmonella** in milk is detected by stool/milk culture or selective media, not the milk ring test.

question: Indian tick typhus is caused by:
explanation:
**Indian tick typhus** is a rickettsial infection caused by *Rickettsia conorii*, a member of the **spotted fever group** of rickettsiae. It is transmitted to humans through the bite of the **brown dog tick (*Rhipicephalus sanguineus*)**, which serves as both vector and reservoir. Clinically, the disease is characterized by fever, a characteristic **eschar (tache noire)** at the site of the tick bite, regional lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash that may involve the palms and soles. The underlying pathology involves rickettsial invasion of **vascular endothelial cells**, causing widespread vasculitis, which explains the rash and systemic manifestations.

The other options are incorrect for the following reasons: ***R. typhi*** (option A) causes **endemic/murine typhus**, transmitted by rat fleas, belonging to the typhus group. ***R. akari*** (option C) causes **rickettsialpox**, transmitted by mites and characterized by a vesicular rash. ***Coxiella burnetii*** (option D) causes **Q fever**, which is typically acquired by inhalation of aerosols from infected animals and notably does **not** produce a rash, distinguishing it from the spotted fever group.

question: PLET medium is used in ?

**PLET medium** (Polymyxin-Lysozyme-EDTA-Thallous acetate) is a selective culture medium specifically used for the isolation of *Bacillus anthracis*, the causative organism of **Anthrax**, particularly from contaminated specimens like animal products, soil, or environmental samples where mixed flora is present.

The selective agents in PLET work by suppressing competing organisms: **polymyxin** inhibits Gram-negative bacteria, **lysozyme** acts against other Gram-positive contaminants, **EDTA** chelates ions to restrict bacterial growth, and **thallous acetate** further suppresses unwanted flora. This combination allows *B. anthracis* colonies to be selectively isolated, where they appear as characteristic non-hemolytic, "medusa-head" or "curled-hair lock" colonies.

The other options are incorrect because they use different media: **Plague** (*Yersinia pestis*) is cultured on blood agar or MacConkey agar showing "stalactite growth" in ghee broth. **Typhoid** (*Salmonella typhi*) uses selective media like Wilson-Blair (bismuth sulphite) agar, DCA, or Selenite F broth. **Cholera** (*Vibrio cholerae*) is grown on TCBS agar (yellow colonies) and enriched in alkaline peptone water.

question: Varicella zoster virus belongs to which family of DNA viruses ?
explanation:
Varicella zoster virus (VZV), also designated human herpesvirus type 3 (HHV-3), is a member of the **Herpesviridae** family, specifically the alphaherpesvirus subfamily. Like all herpesviruses, it is a large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus with an icosahedral capsid, and it possesses the characteristic ability to establish **latency** in sensory (dorsal root) ganglia after primary infection.

Clinically, this explains its dual disease presentation: primary infection causes **chickenpox (varicella)**, after which the virus remains dormant in nerve ganglia and can reactivate years later as **herpes zoster (shingles)**, typically in a dermatomal distribution. This latency-reactivation cycle is a hallmark feature shared with other alphaherpesviruses like HSV-1 and HSV-2.

The other options are incorrect: **Poxviridae** are the largest DNA viruses and replicate in the cytoplasm (e.g., smallpox, molluscum contagiosum); **Adenoviridae** are non-enveloped DNA viruses causing respiratory and conjunctival infections; and **Papovaviridae** (now split into Papillomaviridae and Polyomaviridae) are small non-enveloped DNA viruses associated with warts and certain malignancies. None of these establish ganglionic latency or cause the varicella-zoster spectrum of disease.

question: Smallest Virus is ?

**Parvovirus** is the smallest known DNA virus, measuring approximately **18–26 nm** in diameter. Its name is derived from the Latin word *parvus*, meaning "small," reflecting this defining characteristic. Parvoviruses are non-enveloped, icosahedral viruses containing a single-stranded linear DNA genome, which is among the smallest genomes of all DNA viruses. The clinically important human pathogen is **Parvovirus B19**, which causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease/"slapped cheek" appearance), aplastic crisis in patients with hemolytic anemias (e.g., sickle cell disease), and hydrops fetalis when transmitted transplacentally.

The other options are all larger DNA viruses: **Poxvirus** (option D) is in fact the **largest** virus, measuring about 200–400 nm, large enough to be seen under light microscopy. **Herpesvirus** (option A) is a large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus (~120–200 nm), and **Adenovirus** (option B) is a medium-sized (~70–90 nm), non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus. Therefore, among the given choices, Parvovirus is unequivocally the smallest.

question: DNA polymerase of HBV is encoded by which of the following ?
explanation:
The Hepatitis B virus (HBV) genome is a partially double-stranded circular DNA containing four overlapping open reading frames (ORFs): S, C, P, and X. The **P gene** is the largest ORF and encodes the viral DNA polymerase, which also possesses reverse transcriptase and RNase H activity. This is clinically significant because HBV replicates through an RNA intermediate (pregenomic RNA) that is reverse-transcribed back into DNA—making the polymerase a key target for antiviral nucleoside/nucleotide analogues like tenofovir, entecavir, and lamivudine.

The **S gene** (option A) encodes the surface antigen (HBsAg), including the pre-S1, pre-S2, and S proteins, which form the viral envelope and are the basis of the hepatitis B vaccine. The **C gene** (option B) encodes the core antigen (HBcAg) and, via the precore region, the secreted e antigen (HBeAg), a marker of high infectivity and active replication. The **X gene** (option D) encodes the HBx protein, a transcriptional transactivator implicated in hepatocellular carcinoma development, but it does not encode the polymerase. Therefore, the P gene is the correct answer for the enzyme responsible for HBV genome replication.

question: Which prion disease affect human ?
explanation:
**Kuru** is a prion disease that exclusively affects humans, historically seen among the Fore tribe of Papua New Guinea due to ritualistic cannibalism (consumption of infected brain tissue of the deceased). It is caused by misfolded prion proteins (PrP^Sc) that induce conversion of normal cellular prion protein (PrP^C) into the abnormal form, leading to progressive neurodegeneration, spongiform changes, and cerebellar dysfunction (ataxia, tremors, and the characteristic "laughing death").

The other options are prion diseases that primarily affect animals. **Scrapie** (option A) is a prion disease of sheep and goats. **Bovine spongiform encephalopathy** (option D) and its colloquial name **Mad cow disease** (option B) are the same condition affecting cattle. While BSE can cross to humans causing variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) through consumption of infected beef, BSE itself is an animal disease—making Kuru the only option that is intrinsically a *human* prion disorder.

question: Sabin feldman Dye test is used to demonstrate infection with ?
explanation:
The Sabin-Feldman Dye test is a classic serological assay developed specifically for the diagnosis of **Toxoplasma gondii** infection, making option B correct. It is considered the gold standard reference test for detecting anti-Toxoplasma antibodies.

The underlying principle relies on complement-mediated lysis: live *Toxoplasma* tachyzoites are incubated with the patient's serum. If specific antibodies are present (along with a complement-like accessory factor), they damage the parasite's cytoplasmic membrane, rendering the organism unable to take up the methylene blue dye. Thus, **unstained (colorless) tachyzoites indicate a positive result**, while organisms from antibody-negative serum readily stain blue. This test detects predominantly IgG antibodies and becomes positive 1-2 weeks after infection.

The other options are diagnosed by entirely different methods: **Filaria** (A) is detected by demonstrating microfilariae in nocturnal peripheral blood smears or by antigen detection. **Histoplasma** (C) is identified via fungal culture, histopathology (intracellular yeast in macrophages), or antigen testing. **Ascaris** (D) is diagnosed by finding characteristic ova in stool microscopy. None of these utilize the dye-exclusion serological principle of the Sabin-Feldman test.

question: True about cryptococcus are all except
explanation:
**Cryptococcus neoformans is urease POSITIVE**, making option B the correct "exception" (i.e., the false statement). Urease production is a key identifying biochemical feature of *Cryptococcus*, and it also serves as a virulence factor that aids in crossing the blood-brain barrier, contributing to its tropism for the central nervous system.

Mechanistically, *Cryptococcus* is an encapsulated yeast that is acquired by **inhalation**, so the lung is the primary site of infection (option A is true)—pulmonary cryptococcosis can later disseminate, especially in immunocompromised hosts like AIDS patients, causing meningitis. The thick polysaccharide capsule is demonstrated by the classic **India-ink preparation**, which reveals a clear halo around the yeast against the dark background (option C is true). Because A and C are correct and B is incorrect, option D ("All are true") is also false.

In summary, the only false statement is that *Cryptococcus* is urease negative; it is in fact urease positive, a fact frequently tested in NEET PG microbiology.

question: Bifringence polarization microscopy is used for ?
explanation:
Birefringence (polarization) microscopy detects anisotropic structures that rotate the plane of polarized light, making it ideal for identifying ordered intracellular components and deposits. This technique is particularly valuable for visualizing crystalline or fibrillar intracellular structures, such as amyloid deposits (which show characteristic apple-green birefringence with Congo red staining), monosodium urate crystals (negative birefringence in gout), and calcium pyrophosphate crystals (positive birefringence in pseudogout).

The underlying mechanism relies on the fact that materials with organized molecular arrangements (anisotropic substances) split light into two rays travelling at different velocities, producing distinct optical patterns under crossed polarizers; isotropic structures do not exhibit this property. This allows precise identification of intracellular crystalline material and characterization of fiber orientation in tissues like collagen and muscle.

In contrast, flagella (A) are best demonstrated by special silver-impregnation stains or flagellar staining due to their thinness. Capsules (C) are visualized using negative staining methods like India ink or capsule stains such as the Maneval technique. Spores (D) require specialized stains like the Schaeffer-Fulton (malachite green) method to penetrate their resistant coats. None of these bacterial structures depend on birefringence for visualization, making intracellular crystalline structures the correct application.

question: Acquire IgA deficiency may occur in ?
explanation:
Acquired (secondary) IgA deficiency can result from certain congenital intrauterine infections, and severe congenital toxoplasmosis is a recognized cause among the TORCH group of infections. In congenital toxoplasmosis, the transplacental infection during fetal development interferes with the normal maturation and class-switching of B lymphocytes, leading to impaired production of IgA, the predominant mucosal immunoglobulin. This results in a transient or persistent reduction in serum and secretory IgA levels, making affected infants more susceptible to mucosal and respiratory infections. The underlying mechanism involves the disruptive effect of the intrauterine infection on the developing immune system rather than an inherited genetic defect, distinguishing it from primary IgA deficiency.

In contrast, severe measles infection is classically associated with transient immunosuppression and lymphopenia (suppression of cell-mediated immunity), not a specific IgA deficiency. Brucellosis and leptospirosis are bacterial/spirochetal infections that cause systemic illness but do not characteristically produce acquired IgA deficiency. Therefore, among the given options, severe congenital toxoplasmosis is the correct answer linked to acquired IgA deficiency.

question: Neutrilization test is
explanation:
The Nagler reaction is a classic example of a **neutralization test**, used to identify *Clostridium perfringens* based on its alpha toxin (lecithinase) activity. In this test, the bacteria are inoculated onto an egg yolk agar plate, half of which is pre-treated with specific *C. perfringens* antitoxin. On the untreated half, the lecithinase enzyme breaks down lecithin producing a zone of opacity (turbidity), whereas on the antitoxin-treated half, the antibody **neutralizes** the toxin and inhibits opacity formation. This selective inhibition by specific antiserum is the defining principle of a neutralization test, where antibody counteracts the biological activity of a toxin or enzyme.

The other options operate by different immunological principles. The **Widal test** (option A) and **Weil-Felix test** (option B) are both **agglutination tests** — Widal detects antibodies against *Salmonella* O and H antigens in enteric fever, while Weil-Felix uses *Proteus* OX antigens to detect rickettsial infections through cross-reacting antibodies. The **Paul-Bunnell test** (option C) is a **heterophile agglutination test** detecting antibodies against sheep RBCs in infectious mononucleosis (EBV infection). Since none of these involve neutralizing a toxin's biological effect, the Nagler reaction is the correct answer.

question: IgE binds to which cell ?
explanation:
IgE binds to mast cells (and basophils) through high-affinity Fcε receptors (FcεRI) present on their surface, which is the central event in type I hypersensitivity reactions. When allergen cross-links the IgE molecules already bound to these receptors, it triggers degranulation and release of preformed mediators like histamine, along with newly synthesized leukotrienes and prostaglandins. This mechanism underlies allergic conditions such as asthma, anaphylaxis, urticaria, and atopic reactions. 

T cells (option A) recognize antigen via the T-cell receptor and MHC molecules, not through IgE binding. B cells (option B) produce antibodies including IgE but express surface immunoglobulin (mainly IgM/IgD) as their receptor rather than binding free IgE via Fc receptors. NK cells (option D) carry low-affinity Fcγ receptors (CD16) and mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity using IgG, not IgE. Thus, mast cells are the characteristic cells that bind IgE with high affinity, making option C correct.

question: Which of the following Staphylococcal infection is not toxin mediated:
explanation:
Septic shock caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* results from a systemic inflammatory response to the bacteria themselves (bacteremia) and their cell wall components, rather than from a specific exotoxin. The host's overwhelming immune reaction—driven by cytokine release in response to invading organisms and components like peptidoglycan—leads to vasodilation, hypotension, and organ dysfunction, making it an infection-mediated, not toxin-mediated, process.

In contrast, the other three options are classic toxin-mediated staphylococcal diseases. Toxic shock syndrome (option A) is caused by **TSST-1** (and sometimes enterotoxins) acting as superantigens, which non-specifically activate large numbers of T-cells and cause massive cytokine release. Scalded skin syndrome (option B) results from **exfoliative (epidermolytic) toxins A and B**, which cleave desmoglein-1 in the epidermis, causing superficial skin separation. Staphylococcal food poisoning (option C) is due to preformed, heat-stable **enterotoxins** (commonly enterotoxin A) that cause rapid-onset vomiting and diarrhea. Thus, septic shock is the odd one out as it is driven by the bacterial infection and immune response rather than a defined toxin.

question: Active and passive immunity should be given together in all except -
explanation:
Combined active and passive immunization (giving both a vaccine and preformed antibodies/immunoglobulin simultaneously) is used when immediate protection is needed alongside long-term immunity, typically after exposure to a pathogen with a defined incubation period. Measles is the exception because post-exposure prophylaxis relies on **either** the measles vaccine (if given within 72 hours of exposure) **or** immunoglobulin (within 6 days), but they are **not given together at the same site/time**—passive antibodies would neutralize the live attenuated vaccine virus, blunting the active immune response.

In **tetanus**, after a contaminated wound, tetanus toxoid (active) and tetanus immunoglobulin (passive) are given together at different sites to provide immediate neutralization plus durable immunity. In **rabies**, post-exposure prophylaxis combines rabies vaccine with rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated around the wound, since the long incubation period allows active immunity to develop while passive antibodies offer early protection. In **hepatitis B**, neonates born to HBsAg-positive mothers and exposed individuals receive both the HBV vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) simultaneously. Thus, simultaneous active-passive immunization is standard for tetanus, rabies, and hepatitis B, but contraindicated as a combined regimen in measles.

question: Isolation is not done in ?
explanation:
Mumps does not require isolation because by the time the characteristic parotid swelling appears and the diagnosis is made, the patient has already been infectious for several days, making isolation ineffective in preventing transmission. The virus is spread by respiratory droplets and is communicable from about 6–7 days before to roughly 9 days after the onset of parotitis, so the contagious period largely precedes clinical recognition. Therefore, the emphasis in mumps control is on prevention through MMR vaccination rather than isolation of cases.

In contrast, **Cholera** requires isolation/enteric precautions because it spreads via the fecal-oral route through contaminated water and the patient passes large volumes of infectious stool. **Diphtheria** demands strict isolation until two consecutive negative throat swabs are obtained, as it spreads by respiratory droplets and untreated patients remain infectious. **Hepatitis** (particularly hepatitis A and E) requires enteric precautions, while hepatitis B and C warrant blood/body fluid precautions to prevent transmission. Thus, among the options, mumps is the condition where isolation is not practiced.

In vector born diseases, an arthropod or any living carrier (e.g.,

Agent undergoes only development → Change in form.
No multiplication → No change in number.
Example → Micorfilaria in mosquito.
iii) Cyclo-propagative
Agent undergoes both development and multiplication → Change in
form and number.

Descriptive studies help to suggest an aetiological hypothesis.
Analytic and experimental studies test the hypothesis, derived from

between suspected causes and disease.
Association may be defined as the concurrence of two variables
more often than would be expected by chance. 
In other words, events are said to be associated when they occur
more frequently togeher than one would expect by chance.
Association can be of following types : -
1 .Spurious association
Observed association between a disease and suspected factor is
spurious, i.e., not real.
In other words there is an observed association when none actually
exists.
2.Indirect association
The indirect association is a statistical association between a
variable of interest and a disease due to the presence of another
factor, known or unknown, that is common to both the variable and
the disease.
This third factor (i.e., the common factor) is also known as the
confounding variable.
For example, endemic goitre (disease) is found at high altitudes
(variable), showing thereby an association between altitude and
endemic goitre. But it is due to iodine deficiency which is common at
high altitude. So, iodine deficiency acts as a confounding factor as it
is associated with both high altitude and endemic goitre.
3.Direct (causal) association
a) One to one causal relationship
Two variables are stated to be causally related if change in one is
followed by change in other.
If It does not, then their relationship cannot be causal.
b) Multifactorial causation
The causal thinking is different in non-communicable disease (e.g.,
CHD) where the etiology is multifactorial, i.e., more than one factors
are associated with disease causation.

question: Example of case control study (risk factor and disease/outcome) ?

options.B: Vaginal adenocarcinoma and intrauterine exposure to DES

explanation:
Case-control studies are observational, retrospective designs that begin with the **outcome (disease)** and look backward to identify prior **exposure (risk factor)**. They are particularly valuable for studying **rare diseases** and conditions with **long latency periods**, making them ideal for the scenarios listed. All three examples fit this design: maternal smoking with congenital malformation, vaginal (clear cell) adenocarcinoma with intrauterine DES exposure, and thalidomide exposure with limb teratogenicity (phocomelia)—each involves a relatively uncommon outcome traced back to a suspected antenatal exposure.

The classic landmark example is **DES (diethylstilbestrol)**: by comparing young women with the rare vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma (cases) against unaffected controls, investigators discovered the common factor was their mothers' in-utero DES use, beautifully illustrating the case-control approach. Similarly, the **thalidomide** tragedy was linked to phocomelia through retrospective exposure analysis, and maternal smoking's association with malformations has been studied the same way.

Since options A, B, and C are each individually valid examples of the case-control framework, none can be excluded—hence **D (All of the above)** is correct. The key takeaway is that case-control studies allow calculation of the **odds ratio** (not relative risk, since incidence cannot be directly measured) to estimate the strength of association between exposure and outcome.

question: Matching is not required in which epidemiological study?
explanation:
**Case report** is the correct answer because it is a purely descriptive study describing a single patient or a unique clinical observation, with no comparison or control group involved. Since matching is a technique used specifically to control confounding variables by ensuring comparison groups are similar with respect to certain characteristics (e.g., age, sex), it is irrelevant in a study that has no comparison group at all.

The underlying reasoning is that matching is an analytical tool needed only when two or more groups are being compared, to prevent confounders from distorting the association between exposure and outcome. A case report simply documents what was observed in one or a few cases without statistical comparison, so confounding control through matching does not apply.

In contrast, a **case-control study** frequently uses matching to balance confounders between cases (diseased) and controls (non-diseased). A **cohort study** may also employ matching to ensure exposed and unexposed groups are comparable. A **randomized controlled trial** uses randomization—and sometimes matched designs or stratification—to achieve comparability between intervention and control arms. Therefore, all options except the case report involve comparison groups where matching can be relevant.

question: Relationship between positive predictive value and prevalence ?
explanation:
Positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability that a person who tests positive truly has the disease. PPV is directly proportional to prevalence (option A): as the prevalence of a disease in a population increases, the proportion of true positives among all positive results rises, thereby increasing the PPV.

The underlying mechanism lies in the composition of test-positive individuals. When prevalence is high, there are more true positives relative to false positives, so a positive result is more likely to reflect actual disease. Conversely, in a low-prevalence setting, even a highly specific test yields proportionally more false positives, lowering the PPV. This is why the same diagnostic test performs better (higher PPV) in high-risk or symptomatic populations and worse in screening of low-risk general populations. Importantly, sensitivity and specificity remain intrinsic to the test and do not change with prevalence, but PPV and NPV do.

Options B and D are incorrect because PPV does not vary inversely with prevalence—that inverse relationship actually applies to negative predictive value (NPV α 1/Prevalence). Option C represents a meaningless mathematical equality with no epidemiological basis, as PPV and prevalence are not reciprocals of one another.

question: Which drug is not included in RNTCP regime for MDR TB ?
explanation:
Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) was traditionally considered a Group 5 (reserve) anti-TB drug and was historically not part of the standard RNTCP MDR-TB regimen, which prioritized more effective and better-tolerated agents. The conventional RNTCP regimen for MDR-TB included a fluoroquinolone, an injectable agent (kanamycin/amikacin/capreomycin), and core second-line oral bacteriostatic drugs like ethionamide and cycloserine, along with pyrazinamide and ethambutol.

Cycloserine (option A) is a key second-line oral bacteriostatic drug that inhibits cell wall synthesis and is a standard component of the MDR-TB regimen. Ethionamide (option B), a prothionamide-related agent that inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, is also routinely included as part of the core regimen. Levofloxacin (option C), a later-generation fluoroquinolone, is a crucial bactericidal backbone drug for MDR-TB treatment. PAS, being weakly bacteriostatic and poorly tolerated due to gastrointestinal side effects, was relegated to a reserve role and used only when other drugs could not be employed—making it the agent not routinely included in the standard regimen.

Some definitions of tuberculosis cases and treatment
Case of tuberculosis : A patient in whom tuberculosis has been
confirmed by bacteriology or diagnosed by a clinician.
Sputum smear examination - Laboratory technique to screen sputum
for tuberculosis, where acid fast bacilli (AFB) are stained red by the
Ziehl Neelsen method, and then identified and counted.
using microscopy.
Smear positive tuberculosis - At least one initial sputum smears
positive for AFB or one AFB positive.
Smear negative tuberculosis - At least two negative smears, but
tuberculosis suggestive symptoms and X-ray abnormalities or
positive culture.
Adherence - Person takes appropriate drug regimen for required
time (also known as compliance).
New case - A patient with sputum positive pulmonary tuberculosis
who has never had treatment for tuberculosis or has taken anti -
tuberculosis drugs for less than 4 weeks.
Relapse - A patient who returns smear positive having previously
been treated for tuberculosis and declared cured after the
completion of his treatment.
Failure case - A patient who was initially smear positive, who began
treatment and who remained or became mear positive again at five
months or later during the course of treatment.
Return after default - A patient who returns sputum smear positive,
after having left treatment for at least two months.
Transfer in - A patient recorded in another administrative area
register and transferred into another area to continue treatment
(treatment results should be reported to the district where the patient
was initially registered). Transfer out - A patient who has been
transferred to another area register and treatment results are not
known. Cured - Initially smear positive patient who completed
treatment and had negative smear result on at least two occasions
(one at treatment completion).
Treatment completed - Initially smear negative patient who received
full course of treatment, or smear positive who completed treatment,
with negative smear at the end of initial phase, but no or only one
negative smear during continuation and none at treatment end.
Cohort - A group of patients in whom TB has been diagnosed, and
who were registered for treatment during a specified time period
(e.g. the cohort of new smear-positive cases registered in the
calender year 2003). This group forms the denominator for
calculating treatment outcomes. The sum of the treatment
outcomes, plus any case for which no outcome is recorded (eg. still
on treatment) should equal the number of cases registered.
Case detection rate : - The case detection rate is calculated as the
number of notification of new and relapse cases in a year divided by
the estimated incidence of such cases in the same year.

question: Secondary attack rate of chickenpox ?
explanation:
Chickenpox (varicella) is one of the most highly contagious viral infections, with a secondary attack rate of approximately **90%** among susceptible household contacts, making option B correct. The secondary attack rate measures the proportion of exposed susceptible individuals who develop infection following contact with a primary case, and it reflects both the infectivity of the organism and the closeness of contact.

The varicella-zoster virus spreads efficiently through respiratory droplets and direct contact with vesicular fluid, and the prolonged infectious period (1–2 days before rash until all lesions crust) facilitates near-universal transmission in close settings like households. This exceptionally high attack rate explains why nearly all unvaccinated, non-immune family members of an index case acquire the disease.

Options A (70%), C (65%), and D (80%) underestimate the contagiousness of chickenpox; while these figures may approximate the secondary attack rates of other infections, they are too low for varicella, which classically demonstrates the ~90% figure in standard epidemiology references.

question: Most common type of polio is ?
explanation:
Poliovirus infection most commonly manifests as **inapparent (subclinical) infection**, accounting for approximately 90–95% of all infections. In these cases, the virus replicates in the gut and lymphoid tissue, eliciting a protective immune (antibody) response without producing any clinical symptoms—these individuals are silent carriers who can still shed virus and transmit infection. This high ratio of inapparent to clinical cases (estimated at around 1000:1 in children) is the basis for why polio spreads silently in communities, making surveillance and immunization critical for control.

The other options represent progressively less common, more symptomatic outcomes. **Abortive poliomyelitis (minor illness, ~4–8%)** presents as a nonspecific febrile illness with sore throat, malaise, and gastrointestinal symptoms, without CNS involvement. **Non-paralytic polio (~1%)** progresses to aseptic meningitis with neck stiffness but no paralysis. **Paralytic polio is the rarest form (~0.1–1%)**, resulting from viral invasion of anterior horn motor neurons causing flaccid, asymmetric paralysis—it is the most clinically dramatic but least frequent presentation.

question: Cluster testing technique is useful in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Cluster testing is an epidemiological technique used in **contact tracing**, where an index case is asked to name others who may be part of the same risk-sharing social or sexual network. This method is particularly valuable in **sexually transmitted diseases (STDs)**, including HIV, syphilis, and gonorrhea, because transmission occurs through identifiable sexual or close-contact networks rather than casual exposure.

The underlying principle is that infected individuals share a common cluster of contacts who are at high risk; by tracing not just direct sexual partners but also social contacts within the same high-risk group, asymptomatic or hidden cases can be detected and treated, breaking the chain of transmission. This is especially important for STDs given the social stigma, the existence of hidden reservoirs of infection, and the presence of asymptomatic carriers.

The other options spread differently and are not suited to cluster testing. **Poliomyelitis (B)** and **measles (C)** are transmitted via feco-oral and respiratory (airborne droplet) routes respectively, affecting communities broadly rather than through defined risk-sharing networks, and are controlled mainly through **immunization and herd immunity**. **Smallpox (D)** was eradicated through **surveillance and containment (ring vaccination)**, not cluster testing of social contacts in the STD sense.

question: Prevalence of HIV infection in antenatal women is less than 1% and in high risk population is less than 5%. The state belongs to ?
explanation:
India's NACO (National AIDS Control Organisation) classifies states/districts into four groups based on HIV surveillance data from antenatal clinics (ANC) and high-risk groups (HRGs), which guides resource allocation and intervention strategies. **Group III** is defined by HIV prevalence of **less than 1% in antenatal women AND less than 5% in high-risk populations**, indicating low prevalence in the general population but with a vulnerable high-risk segment that has not yet reached the critical threshold.

The classification reflects the epidemiological trajectory of the infection — antenatal prevalence serves as a proxy for spread into the general population, while HRG prevalence (sex workers, IDUs, MSM) signals concentrated epidemics that could potentially bridge into the wider community.

**Group I** is high prevalence: HIV >1% in ANC women (established generalised epidemic). **Group II** is concentrated epidemic with HIV <1% in ANC but ≥5% in high-risk groups, signalling active transmission within vulnerable populations that threatens broader spread. **Group IV** represents the lowest risk category: <1% in ANC women and <5% in HRGs, but additionally with **no detection or very low prevalence among high-risk groups**, distinguishing it from Group III where the HRG component remains a defined concern.

question: All are true about epidemiological features of cholera except ?

options.B: Poor sanitation is cause of epidemic
options.C: El Tor biotype has decreased endemicity

explanation:
The El Tor biotype of *Vibrio cholerae* is associated with **increased endemicity**, not decreased, making option C the exception and the correct answer. El Tor causes a higher proportion of subclinical and mild infections (a high carrier-to-case ratio of about 1:10 or more), allowing the organism to persist and circulate silently in the community, which sustains endemic transmission. Additionally, El Tor survives longer in the environment and in carriers, further enhancing its ability to establish endemicity compared to the classical biotype.

Regarding the other options: (A) cholera epidemics are indeed **self-limiting**, typically subsiding within a few weeks to months as susceptible individuals are exhausted and immunity develops. (B) **Poor sanitation and contaminated water supply** are classic risk factors, since cholera spreads via the feco-oral route through contaminated food and water. (D) The onset of a cholera epidemic is characteristically **abrupt or explosive**, owing to a short incubation period (few hours to 5 days) and a common-source (waterborne) mode of transmission. Thus, all features except the claim about El Tor decreasing endemicity are true.

indicates recovery and end of period of communicability.
Anti-HBe Ag : Its presence indicate stopage of replication and low
infectivity.

question: An epidemiologist visits village and wants to collect data for recent parasitic activity. What should be measure ?
explanation:
Infant parasite rate
MEASUREMENT OF MALARIA
In the pre-eradication era, the magnitude of the malaria problem in a
country used to be determined mostly from the reports of the
clinically diagnosed malaria cases and the classical malariometric
measures, e.g., spleen rate, parasite rate etc.
On the other hand, during eradication era, the microscopic diagnosis
of malaria cases became the main method of diagnosis and the
parameters used are mostly parasitological in nature e.g., API,
ABER, SPR and SFR.
Measurements of malaria in the pre eradication era
a) Spleen rate:
Defined as the percentage of children between 2 & 10 years of age
showing enlargement of spleen. Spleen rate is widely used for
measuring the endemicity of malaria in a community.
b) Av. enlarged spleen :
A refinement of spleen rate , denoting the average size of spleen.
c) Parasite rate :
Defined as on the percentage of children between the ages of 2 &
10 yrs showing malarial parsites in their blood films.
d) Parasite density index :
Average degree of parasitimia
e) Infant parasite rate
Percentage of infants showing malarial parasites in their blood films.
It is the most sensitive index of recent transmission of malaria in a
locality. If the infant parasite rate is zero for three consecutive years
in a locality, it is regarded as absence of malaria transmission even
though, the Anopheline vectors responsible for previous
transmissions may remain.
Eradication Era
a) Annual Parasite Incidence (API)*
= (Confirmed cases during one year / population under surveillance)
x 1000
b) Annual Blood Examination Rate = (No. of slides
examined/population) x 100
ABER is an index of operational efficiency.
In the modified plan of operation, the minimum prescribed is 10
percent of the population in a year
c) Annual falciparum index
d) Slide positivity rate
Slide positivity rate is the percentage of slides found positive for
malarial parasite, irrespective of the type of species.
Slide falciparum rate
It is the percentage of slides positive for P. falciparum.

question: An american wants prophylaxis for Hepatitis-A before coming to India for 10 days. What should be given ?
explanation:
Immunoglobulin
Advice for travellers
Some of the recommendation pertain to the following :?
1. Avoid bathing with polluted water as this may result in ear, eye and
skin infections. Excessive heat and humidity or over-exertion in
these conditions may lead to exhaustion from loss of water and salt.
2. The measures for prevention of insect bites.
3. Diarrhoeal Diseases : "Be careful what you eat" is common advice to
travellers, but very few truely understand its implications. Diarrhoea
affects an estimated 20-50 per cent of all travellers. Contaminated
food drinks are the most common source of these infections. Careful
selection and preparation of food and drink offer the best protection.
Unfortunately appearance of food is no guide as to its safety. The
main personal proection is to consider unpasteurized milk, non-
bottled drinks, uncooked food (apart from the fruits and vegetables
that can be peeled or shelled), as likely to be contaminated and
therefore unsafe. The food should be throughly and freshly cooked.
Use boiled water or bottled mineral water (now available
everywhere). Travellers should be aware of the importance of oral
rehydration fluids containing salt and glucose for countering
dehydration.
4. Malaria : There is a high risk of acquiring malaria in endemic areas.
Travellers are advised to protect themselves by chemoprophylaxis.
Drug prophylaxis should begin at the latest on the day of arrival in
the malarious areas and continued for 4-6 weeks after leaving the
malarious areas.
5. Hepatitis A : Normal human immunoglobulin in a dose of 0.02-0.05
mg/kg of body weight has been recommended every 4 months.
Ideally immunoglobulin should not be given within 3 weeks before,
or untill 2 weeks after administration of a live vaccine. A highly safe,
inactivated HAV vaccine is available in several European countries.
6. Hepatitis E : There is no vaccine against hepatitis E and
immunoglobulin prepared in Europe and USA does not give much of
protection. Avoidence of contaminated food and water is the only
effective protective measure.
7. Hepatitis B : Hepatitis B vaccines are available and are safe. Three
doses of vaccine constitute the complete course. The first two doses
are given one month apart and the third dose about 6 months later.
8. STD and HIV : Measures for preventing STD are the same whether
the individual is travelling abroad or not, i.e. avoidance of sex
altogether or limit it to a single faithful, uninfected partner. Use of
condom is an important preventive measure. To reduce the risk of
acquiring HIV and hepatitis B from syringes and needles, travellers
should avoid injectable drugs and if an injection is essential they
should make sure that the needle and syringe come from sterile
pack.
9. Yellow fever : Vaccination certificate for yellow fever is the only
certificate required for international travel. Yellow fever vaccine is
recommended for travellers to countires designated as yellow fever
endemic zone.
10. Tetanus : It is a wise precaution for the traveller to have a booster
dose of tetanus toxoid if 10 years or more have elapsed since the
last injection of a complete course or booster.

specified in the "International health regulation" of WHO.
These are implemented by the Govt of India through stringent aerial
and maritime traffic regulations.

 Revaccination performed before the end of the validity of certicicate

area.
ii) Mosquitoes
The aircraft and ships arriving from endemic areas are subjected to
aerosol spraying with prescribed insecticides.
Airports and Seaports are kept free from the breeding of insect
vectors over an area extending at least 400 metres around their
perimeters.
The "aedes aegypti index" is kept below 1.

question: Not a copper containing IUD ?
explanation:
LNG-20 (Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, commercially known as Mirena) is **not** a copper-containing IUD; instead, it is a hormonal intrauterine device that releases the progestin levonorgestrel (20 µg/day), making option D correct.

Unlike copper devices that work primarily by creating a spermicidal, inflammatory intrauterine environment, LNG-20 acts by thickening cervical mucus (impeding sperm penetration), causing endometrial atrophy/suppression, and partially inhibiting ovulation. Its hormonal action also reduces menstrual blood loss, which is why it is therapeutically used for menorrhagia, in contrast to copper IUDs that often increase menstrual bleeding.

The remaining options are all copper-bearing devices: **CuT-200** is a first-generation copper-T carrying 200 mm² of copper surface area, **Multiload-250** carries 250 mm² of copper, and **Nova-T** contains copper with a silver core to prevent fragmentation and prolong effectiveness. Since all three rely on copper ions for their contraceptive effect, only LNG-20 stands apart as a hormonal, non-copper IUD.

question: Contraception with increased risk of actinomycosis ?
explanation:
**IUCD (Intrauterine Contraceptive Device)** is strongly associated with an increased risk of pelvic actinomycosis, particularly with prolonged use. *Actinomyces israelii*, a gram-positive, anaerobic, filamentous bacterium that is a normal commensal of the female genital tract, can colonize the foreign surface of the IUCD. The device acts as a nidus, allowing the organism to adhere, proliferate, and form characteristic "sulfur granules," potentially leading to ascending infection and pelvic inflammatory disease. On Pap smear, these organisms may appear as "cotton-wool" or dust-ball colonies, and detection often warrants device removal and antibiotic therapy (penicillin being the drug of choice).

The other options are incorrect because they do not introduce a persistent foreign body into the genital tract. **OCPs** are systemic hormonal agents with no association with actinomycosis—in fact, they reduce PID risk by thickening cervical mucus. **Condoms** are barrier methods that lower the risk of all genital infections, and **vaginal methods** (e.g., diaphragms, spermicides) carry no significant link to actinomycosis since they lack the chronic intrauterine foreign-body effect that promotes colonization.

question: Protein content in F-75 milk formula ?
explanation:
F-75 is the WHO-recommended therapeutic milk formula used in the **initial stabilization phase** of treating children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM). It contains **0.9 gm of protein per 100 ml**, along with 75 kcal of energy per 100 ml (hence the name "F-75"), making option B correct.

The deliberately low protein and energy content is the key clinical principle here. In severely malnourished children, metabolic and organ functions (especially the liver, heart, and kidneys) are compromised, and a high protein/calorie load during early refeeding can precipitate **refeeding syndrome** with dangerous electrolyte shifts (hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia), fluid overload, and cardiac failure. F-75 is therefore low in protein, fat, and sodium but relatively high in carbohydrate to gently restore metabolic function. Once the child is stabilized (typically after the first week), the formula is transitioned to **F-100** (100 kcal and ~2.9 gm protein per 100 ml) to promote rapid catch-up growth.

Options A (0.5 gm) and C (1.5 gm) state incorrect values that do not match the standardized F-75 composition. Option D (2.0 gm per 100 ml) reflects a higher protein content closer to catch-up formulas like F-100 and would be inappropriate—and potentially harmful—during the stabilization phase.

question: Stage of contraction of family starts at ?
explanation:
The family life cycle is divided into distinct stages based on the dynamics of family size and composition. The **contraction stage** begins when the **first child leaves home** (option D), marking the point at which the family unit starts to shrink as grown children depart to establish independent lives. This phase continues until all children have left, culminating in the "empty nest" period and eventually ending with the death of one or both spouses.

The underlying logic follows the natural progression of family demographics: the family expands during the reproductive years and contracts during the dispersal years. The **stage of expansion** starts with marriage (option A) and the birth of children, while the **stage of stabilization** (or completion) occurs with the birth of the last child, when family size reaches its maximum.

Therefore, **marriage (A)** signals the formation/expansion phase, **birth of a child (B)** represents expansion, and **birth of the last child (C)** marks the end of expansion and the beginning of stabilization—not contraction. Only the departure of children (D) reflects the actual reduction in family size that defines contraction.

question: Pulses contain all except ?
explanation:
Pulses (legumes such as lentils, beans, and peas) are deficient in the sulfur-containing amino acids, namely **methionine and cysteine**, which makes option B the correct "except" answer. This deficiency is the defining limitation of pulse proteins and explains why they are considered an incomplete protein source on their own.

The underlying nutritional reasoning lies in **complementary protein action**: pulses are rich in lysine but poor in methionine/cysteine, whereas cereals (rice, wheat) are rich in methionine/cysteine but deficient in lysine. Therefore, combining cereals and pulses (e.g., dal-rice or khichdi) provides a balanced amino acid profile with high biological value—a key concept in Indian dietary planning and prevention of protein malnutrition.

Regarding the other options: **Lysine (A)** is abundant in pulses and is in fact their hallmark amino acid, making them an excellent supplement to lysine-deficient cereals. **Arginine (C)** is also well represented in legume proteins. **Protein (D)** is incorrect as an exception because pulses are among the richest plant sources of protein (around 20–25% by weight), serving as a major protein source in vegetarian diets.

question: Mid-day meals provided in schools provide ?
explanation:
The Mid-Day Meal Programme (now part of the PM POSHAN scheme) is designed to supplement the nutritional needs of school-going children, and its standard guideline is to provide **one-third (1/3) of the daily total caloric requirement and one-half (1/2) of the daily protein requirement**. This makes option B correct. The rationale behind providing a higher proportion of protein relative to calories is that protein-energy malnutrition is highly prevalent among Indian schoolchildren, and protein is the more critical and commonly deficient macronutrient in their diets; thus the program emphasizes protein adequacy. The "one-third calorie" figure reflects that the meal is meant to be a supplement (one of roughly three daily meals), not the child's complete daily intake.

Options A and C are incorrect because the meal does not aim to provide half the total calories—doing so would over-rely on a single supplementary meal. Option D is wrong because while 1/3 calories is accurate, it underestimates protein supplementation (1/4 instead of the correct 1/2), defeating the program's key objective of combating protein deficiency. Remembering the pairing "1/3 calories, 1/2 protein" is the high-yield point for this question.

question: Vitamin deficient in Famines ?
explanation:
**Vitamin A deficiency** is the classic micronutrient deficiency associated with famines, as it is the most common cause of preventable blindness and a major public health problem during food shortages and humanitarian crises. During famines, diets become severely restricted and lack the colored fruits, vegetables, dairy, and animal sources that provide preformed vitamin A (retinol) and provitamin carotenoids.

Mechanistically, vitamin A is essential for the synthesis of **rhodopsin** in retinal rod cells, so its deficiency first manifests as **night blindness (nyctalopia)**, progressing to xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia, and irreversible blindness. It also maintains epithelial integrity and immune function, so deficiency increases susceptibility to infections like measles and diarrhea, raising child mortality during famines. This is why WHO and UNICEF prioritize vitamin A supplementation in famine relief and child survival programs.

The other options are less relevant to famine settings: **Vitamin D (B)** deficiency relates to inadequate sunlight exposure and causes rickets/osteomalacia, not a hallmark of acute famine. **Vitamin B12 (C)** deficiency is typically due to malabsorption (pernicious anemia) or strict veganism rather than general caloric famine. **Vitamin B6 (D)** deficiency is rare and usually drug-induced (e.g., isoniazid), making it an uncommon famine-associated finding.

Chlorination
Chlorination is one of the greatest advances in water purification.
Chlorine kills pathogenic bacteria, but has no effect on spores,
certain viruses (e.g., polio, viral hepatitis) and cyst of E.histolytica, in
usual doses.
Mechanism of action
When chlorine is added to water, there is the formation of
hypochloric and hypochlorous acid
The hypochloric acid is neutralized by the alkalinity of the water.
The hypochlorous acid ionizes to form hydrogen ions and
hypochlorite ions.
The disinfecting action of chlorine is mainly due to the hypochlorous

question: Best way to dispose e-waste is?
explanation:
Recycling
E-Waste
E-waste is a popular, informal name for electronic products nearing
the end of their "useful life.
"E-wastes are considered dangerous, as certain components of
some electronics products contain materials that are hazardous,
depending on their condition and density.
The hazardous content of these materials pose a threat to human
health and environment.
Discarded computers, television, VCRs, stereos, copiers, fax
machines, electric lamps, cell phones, audio equiopment and
batteries if improperly disposed can leach lead and other substances
into soil and groundwater.
Many of these products can be reused, refurbished, or recycled, or
recyled in an environmentally sound manner so that they are less
harmful to the ecosystem.
Managment of E-Waste
In industries management of e-waste should begin at the point of
generation. This can be done by waste minimization techniques and
by sustainable product design. Waste minimization in industries
involves adopting:
1. inventory management,
2. production-process modification,
3. volume reduction,
4. recovery and reuse
Inventory management
Proper control over the materials used in the manufacturing process
is an important way to reduce waste generation.
By reducing both the quantity of hazardous materials used in the
process and the amount of excess raw materials in stock, the
quantity of waste generated can be reduced.
Developing review procedures for all material purchased is the first
stop in establishing an inventory management program.
Another inventory management procedure for waste reduction is to
ensure that only the needed quantity of a material is ordered.
Production-process modification
Changes cna be made in the production process, which will reduce
waste generation.
This reduction can be accomplished by changing the materials used
to make the product or by the more efficient use of input materials in
the production process or both.
Volume reduction
Volume reduction includes those techniques that remove the
hazardous portion of a waste from a non-hazardous portion.
These techniques are usually to reduce the volume, and thus the
cost of disposing of a waste material.
Recovery and reuse
This technique could eliminate waste disposal costs, reduce raw
material costs and provide income from a salable waste.
Waste can be recovered on-site, or at an off-site recovery facility, or
through inter industry exchange.

question: A problem village is one where ?
explanation:
A "problem village" is a public health and rural water supply classification used to identify settlements facing significant difficulties in accessing safe and adequate drinking water. By definition, a village qualifies as a problem village if it meets **any one** of several criteria, which is why option D (All of the above) is correct—each listed condition independently characterizes a problem village.

The criteria include: (1) the source of water being located **more than 1.6 km away** (or more than 100 meters of elevation difference in hilly areas), making access physically arduous; (2) **water available only at depths greater than 15 meters**, indicating difficulty in extraction and limited shallow groundwater; and (3) **excess fluoride or other chemicals** (like arsenic, iron, or salinity) in the water, posing health risks such as dental and skeletal fluorosis. These factors reflect either quantitative inaccessibility or qualitative contamination that compromises safe water availability.

Options A, B, and C are each individually valid definitions but incomplete on their own, since a village meeting only one of these would still be classified as a problem village. Therefore, since all three represent recognized criteria, the comprehensive answer is **D. All of the above**.

question: Most important measure to prevent hospital infection ?
explanation:
Proper hand washing
There are following types of modes of transmission of hospital-
acquired infections :
1) Contact transmission
i. It is the most common and most preventable means of transmission.
It is divided into two types -
ii. Direct contact : It involves contact of body surface to body surface
with a physical transfer of microorganisms. Hand contact is most
common mode of transmission.
iii. Indirect contact : It involves body surface contact with a
contaminated intermediate object.
As hand contact is the most common mode of transmission, the best
preventive measure of nosocomial infection is proper hand hygiene.
2) Droplet transmission
It occurs when droplet containing microorganisms from an infected
person are propelled through the air (e.g. coughing, sneezing) and
land on the mouth, eyes or nose of another person.
3) Airborne transmission
It results when a droplet containing microorganisms evaporates and
remains suspended in air for a long time (this should not be
confused with droplet infection, in which transmission is immediate
and droplets do not remains suspended in the air).
Airborne transmission also occurs by dust particles containing
microorganism.
4) Vehicle transmission
It refers to transmission of infection by contaminated items such as
food, water, medications, devices and equipment.

question: Ujjwala scheme does not include ?
explanation:
The Ujjwala scheme is a comprehensive welfare programme launched by the Ministry of Women and Child Development aimed at the prevention of trafficking and the rescue, rehabilitation, and reintegration of victims of trafficking for commercial sexual exploitation. **Reward (option D) is not a component of this scheme**, as the programme focuses on protecting and restoring the lives of trafficking survivors rather than providing any form of incentive or reward.

The scheme operates through five key components: Prevention, Rescue, Rehabilitation, Reintegration, and Repatriation. **Rescue (option A)** involves safely removing victims from exploitative situations. **Rehabilitation (option B)** provides safe shelter, food, clothing, medical care, legal aid, vocational training, and psychological counselling to help survivors recover. **Reintegration (option C)** focuses on restoring victims back into their families and society, while repatriation addresses returning cross-border victims to their home countries.

Since Reward is absent from the scheme's framework, it is the correct answer. The Ujjwala scheme is rights-based and welfare-oriented, designed to break the cycle of trafficking rather than incentivize any behaviour—making "Reward" conceptually inconsistent with the programme's protective objectives.

question: Which of the following is used to represent continuous (quantitative) data ?
explanation:
**Histogram** is the correct method for representing continuous (quantitative) data because it displays the frequency distribution of variables measured on a continuous scale, such as height, weight, blood pressure, or age. The defining feature of a histogram is that its bars are drawn **adjacent to each other with no gaps**, reflecting the uninterrupted, continuous nature of the underlying data along the x-axis (which represents class intervals). The area of each bar is proportional to the frequency within that class interval, allowing accurate visualization of how values are distributed.

In contrast, a **bar diagram** (option A) is used for **discrete or qualitative (categorical) data**, with distinct bars separated by gaps—each bar represents an independent category. A **pie chart** (option B) depicts qualitative data as proportions or percentages of a whole, suitable for showing the relative contribution of categories rather than continuous measurements. A **map diagram** (option D), or spot/cartogram, is used to display the **geographical distribution** of a disease or event and does not represent continuous numerical data. Thus, only the histogram is appropriate for continuous quantitative data.

question: Which is best to represent the data of following table - Year 1991199219931994 Number 75 125 50 25 of LBW bodies
explanation:
A **bar chart** is the most appropriate method to represent this data because the variable on the X-axis (Year) is **discrete/qualitative in presentation**, while the Y-axis shows the number of low birth weight (LBW) babies for each separate year. Bar charts use rectangular bars with **gaps between them**, which correctly reflects that each year's data is a distinct, non-continuous category rather than a continuous range. This allows easy visual comparison of LBW counts across the four years (75, 125, 50, 25), clearly highlighting trends like the peak in 1992 and decline thereafter.

A **histogram (B)** is incorrect because it is used for **continuous data grouped into class intervals**, with bars drawn adjacent (no gaps); here the years are treated as discrete categories, not continuous intervals. A **frequency polygon (C)** is also meant for continuous quantitative data and is used to show frequency distribution or compare multiple distributions, which is unnecessary for this simple categorical comparison. A **scatter diagram (D)** is used to show the **correlation between two continuous quantitative variables**, not to display frequency counts across discrete time points. Hence, the bar chart best displays this discrete, year-wise comparative data.
